noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that a co-ordinated response requires a stimulus, a receptor and an effector

primer.text: You already know that glands and muscles carry out actions inside the body, and that some of those actions happen without any decision on your part. This note names the three parts every automatic control loop needs: a change that gets detected, a cell that detects it, and the muscle or gland that acts. Master this vocabulary and every later control system becomes a labelled example of the same loop.

lessons.title: The parts of a co-ordinated response
lessons.opening: Whenever conditions inside the body drift away from their ideal level, an automatic loop brings them back. The loop always has the same three components: something changes, a receptor detects that change, and an effector acts to reverse it. Between detection and action sits a coordination centre — the brain, spinal cord or pancreas — which processes the information.
keyPoints: A co-ordinated response needs a stimulus: a change in the environment such as shifted blood glucose or temperature.
Receptors are cells that detect stimuli and pass the information on.
A coordination centre — the brain, spinal cord or pancreas — receives and processes information from receptors.
An effector is a muscle or gland that carries out the response and restores the optimum level.

low.restatement: A change is detected by a receptor, processed by a coordination centre, and reversed by an effector such as a muscle or gland.
low.analogy: It works like a thermostat: the sensor notices the room drifting, the controller decides, and the heater or chiller acts.
low.examPointer: Name all three parts — stimulus, receptor, effector — whenever a question asks how a control system works; missing one costs the mark.

medium.restatement: Involuntary control loops run through the brain stem or spinal cord without conscious effort, linking receptors to effectors through a processing centre to restore set points.
medium.analogy: Picture a factory line where inspectors report faults to a supervisor who directs machine operators to correct them — detection, decision, correction.
medium.examPointer: Questions often plant a distractor claiming conscious control — remember homeostatic loops are automatic, so say involuntary in answers about thermoregulation or water balance.

check.stem: What term describes a change in the environment that triggers a response?

options.explanation: A stimulus is defined as a change in the environment that the body responds to.
Receptors detect the change; they are not the change itself.
Effectors carry out the response, they do not trigger it.
A nephron is a kidney filtering unit, unrelated to the trigger of a response.

check.stem: Which cells detect stimuli in an automatic control system?

options.explanation: Effectors act; they do not detect.
Receptor cells are the detectors of stimuli in a control system.
Red cells transport oxygen, they take no part in detection.
Guard cells open and close stomata in leaves, a plant structure outside this control loop.

check.stem: Where is information from receptors processed during a co-ordinated response?

options.text: In the effector, which then acts directly
options.explanation: Effectors execute; processing happens before they are instructed.

options.text: In the coordination centre — brain, spinal cord or pancreas
options.explanation: The coordination centre receives and processes the receptor information.
A stimulus is a change, not a processing structure.
Blood carries materials, it does not process information.

check.stem: Which of these acts as an effector?

options.explanation: Muscles and glands are the two named effectors.

options.text: A receptor cell in the skin
options.explanation: Skin receptors detect, they do not act.
That is a coordination centre, not an effector.
Sensory neurones transmit signals, they are pathway cells rather than effectors.

check.stem: Which sequence lists the required components of a co-ordinated response in the correct order?

options.text: Receptor, then coordination centre, then effector
options.explanation: This skips the stimulus that starts the loop.
Detection follows the change, and the effector acts last.
That reverses the entire sequence.
The effector cannot act before detection has happened.

check.stem: State the three components every co-ordinated response requires.
check.modelAnswer: A stimulus, a receptor and an effector.

check.stem: Give the collective name for the structures, including the brain and pancreas, that receive and process information from receptors.
check.modelAnswer: Coordination centres — the brain, spinal cord and pancreas are the named examples.

check.stem: Explain why homeostatic responses happen without conscious thought.
check.modelAnswer: They are involuntary: the brain stem and spinal cord run the control loops automatically, so you never decide to start sweating or adjusting water levels — the systems act to keep conditions stable whether or not you are aware of them.

check.stem: After exercise a person's blood glucose concentration falls. Using the control-loop model, identify the stimulus and the kind of structure that acts as the effector here.
check.modelAnswer: The stimulus is the fall in blood glucose below its set level; receptors detect it and the coordination centre directs effectors — glands releasing hormones and the liver releasing stored glucose — until the concentration is restored.

glossary.definition: A change in the internal or external environment that a receptor detects and the body responds to.
A cell that detects a stimulus and passes information on to a coordination centre.
A structure such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas that receives and processes information from receptors.
A muscle or gland that carries out the response which restores optimum conditions.
